articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.1 million in hurricane recovery funds sits unspent a year after Idalia
articles.dek: Federal reimbursement rules and staffing shortages have left debris removal contracts in limbo while residents wait for infrastructure repairs in Cantonment and Bellview.
brief: Escambia County has drawn down less than 12% of the $2.1 million allocated for Hurricane Idalia recovery since August 2025.
FEMA reimbursement requirements and a two-person public works administrative staff have created a backlog of 47 pending debris removal claims.
Residents in Cantonment and Bellview report waiting eight months or longer for road repairs and drainage fixes promised after the storm.
articles.body:
The culvert on Doris Drive in Cantonment collapsed during Hurricane Idalia. That was eleven months ago. Linda Mercer has called the county fourteen times since.

"They told me in October they had the money," Mercer said. "They told me in February it was on the list. Last month they stopped returning my calls."

The money exists. According to county budget documents reviewed by The Flightline, Escambia County received $2.1 million in Federal Emergency Management Agency Public Assistance funds for Idalia recovery in October 2025. As of June 15, the county has spent $247,000.

The rest sits in a dedicated account while 47 debris removal and infrastructure repair claims wait in a processing queue that moves, by the county's own estimate, at roughly four projects per month.

The bottleneck

Escambia County's Public Works Department employs two full-time administrative staff members responsible for federal disaster reimbursement paperwork. Those two employees manage claims not just from Idalia but from lingering Hurricane Sally projects dating to 2020.

"We're working as fast as we can with what we have," said Public Works Director Marcus Thibodaux in an interview. "FEMA doesn't just cut checks. Every dollar has to be documented, justified and approved through their system before we can proceed."

The FEMA Public Assistance program reimburses local governments for disaster response and recovery costs—but only after the work is completed and documented to federal standards. That means Escambia County must often pay contractors upfront, then wait months for reimbursement while navigating a federal bureaucracy that requires detailed cost breakdowns, photographic evidence, environmental reviews and compliance certifications for each project.

"It's not the money," Thibodaux said. "It's the paper."

What's waiting

The Flightline obtained a partial list of pending Idalia recovery projects through a public records request. Among them:

Sixteen road repairs in Cantonment and Bellview, estimated total cost $890,000. Nine drainage and culvert replacements across unincorporated Escambia County, estimated at $540,000. Twenty-two debris removal reimbursement claims from private contractors who cleared fallen trees from rights-of-way in the weeks after the storm.

Those debris contractors have been waiting since fall 2025 for payment. Several have stopped bidding on county work.

"I'm not doing business with Escambia County again until they pay what they owe," said James Fontaine, owner of Fontaine Tree Service in Pace. The county owes his company $67,000 for post-Idalia debris removal, according to invoices he provided. "I've got employees to pay. I can't float the government."

Staffing and priorities

County Administrator Wes Moreno acknowledged the backlog in a June 12 budget workshop but pushed back on characterizations that the county was sitting on money.

"These aren't unspent funds in any meaningful sense," Moreno said. "They're committed. They're allocated. We just have to process them correctly or we don't get reimbursed and taxpayers eat the cost."

When Commissioner Jeff Bergosh asked whether the county could hire additional staff to accelerate processing, Moreno pointed to broader budget constraints. The county faces a projected $3.4 million shortfall in the upcoming fiscal year and has implemented a hiring freeze on non-essential positions.

"We could hire two more people in public works admin," Moreno said. "But then we're cutting somewhere else. That's the trade-off."

The two existing staffers, who declined to be named, earn a combined $94,000 annually. The 47 pending claims represent potential reimbursements worth roughly $1.85 million.

On the ground

In Bellview, the intersection of Mobile Highway and Crabtree Church Road floods during moderate rain. It flooded before Idalia. The storm made it worse. A drainage improvement project has been on the county's capital plan since 2019. Post-Idalia FEMA funds could cover 75% of the estimated $180,000 cost.

The project remains in the queue.

"Every time it rains hard, I'm wondering if I can get to work," said Robert Stallworth, who lives a quarter-mile from the intersection. "The county says they're working on it. That's been the answer for seven years."

Mercer, on Doris Drive, has started driving through her neighbor's yard to avoid the collapsed culvert. Her neighbor hasn't complained yet. She doesn't know how long that will last.

"I'm 68 years old," she said. "I just want to be able to get out of my driveway without worrying my car's going to fall in a hole."

What happens next

FEMA funds for Idalia recovery must be obligated within 18 months of the disaster declaration and spent within 24 months, absent an extension. That gives Escambia County until August 2027 to complete all work—a deadline Thibodaux called "achievable but tight."

"We're not going to leave money on the table," he said. "But I can't promise everyone's project gets done when they want it done."

The county commission will consider a budget amendment at its July 11 meeting that could add one temporary position to assist with federal grant administration. The position would be funded through the FEMA allocation itself, which allows up to 5% of funds to cover administrative costs.

Moreno said the position, if approved, could begin work by August.

For Mercer, that's another two months of driving through her neighbor's yard.

"They've had a year," she said. "What's two more months?"

She paused.

"Everything, honestly. It's everything."

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The last fishing camp on Perdido Key is for sale. What happens next will shape the pass for decades.
articles.dek: A 3-acre parcel near the state park has drawn interest from condo developers and conservation groups alike, reopening old fights about density and public water access.
brief: The Hernandez family is selling their 3-acre fishing camp on Perdido Key after 67 years of continuous operation, with an asking price of $4.2 million.
At least two condominium developers and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection have expressed interest in the property, which includes 180 feet of pass-front shoreline.
The sale has reignited long-standing debates about development density on the barrier island and the shrinking inventory of public water access points.
articles.body:
The bait freezer still hums at Hernandez Fish Camp, though nobody has restocked it in three weeks. A hand-painted sign advertising live shrimp—$6 a scoop—swings from a post near the boat ramp, its letters faded to a shade somewhere between coral and rust. Pelicans line the seawall like they're waiting for something.

They'll be waiting a while longer. After 67 years, the Hernandez family has put the property up for sale.

The 3-acre parcel sits on the bay side of Perdido Key, less than a mile from the entrance to Big Lagoon State Park. It includes 180 feet of shoreline on Perdido Pass, a concrete boat ramp, the original 1959 fish house, and a bungalow where three generations of the Hernandez family have lived. The asking price is $4.2 million.

What happens to those three acres will likely determine whether any working waterfront remains on the developed portion of Perdido Key—and whether the public will retain meaningful access to one of the last natural passes on Florida's Gulf Coast.

'We can't hold it anymore'

Carmen Hernandez, 71, sat on the fish house porch last Tuesday morning, watching mullet jump in the pass. Her father, Miguel Hernandez Sr., bought the land in 1959 for $8,000. He'd come to Pensacola from Cuba two years earlier and worked the shrimp boats out of Joe Patti's before saving enough to buy his own slice of waterfront.

"He wanted a place where working people could fish," Carmen Hernandez said. "That was the whole idea. You didn't need a boat. You didn't need money. You just needed a line."

For decades, the camp operated as an informal public amenity. The Hernandez family charged modest fees—$5 to launch a boat, $3 to fish from the seawall—and sold bait, ice, and cold drinks from the fish house. Commercial fishermen used the dock. Families brought coolers and spent Saturdays casting for redfish.

But the economics stopped working years ago. Property taxes on the parcel have climbed to $47,000 annually, according to Escambia County records. Insurance costs tripled after Hurricane Sally in 2020. Miguel Hernandez Jr., who managed day-to-day operations, died of a heart attack in 2023 at age 68.

"My brother kept this place alive through pure stubbornness," Carmen Hernandez said. "I don't have that in me anymore. We can't hold it."

The interested parties

The listing, handled by Bellview-based commercial broker Mariner Realty, has generated immediate interest.

According to listing agent Tom Weatherford, at least two condominium developers have requested site surveys and zoning information. Weatherford declined to name the developers but confirmed both have built on Perdido Key before.

"This is the last assembleable parcel on the pass side with that kind of frontage," Weatherford said in a phone interview. "Everyone who builds out here knows what that means."

Under current Escambia County zoning, the property is classified as mixed-use coastal, which permits residential density of up to 20 units per acre. A developer could theoretically build 60 condominium units on the site, though wetland setbacks and parking requirements would likely reduce that number.

But developers aren't the only ones circling.

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection has also expressed interest, according to agency spokesperson Linda Castillo. The property borders Big Lagoon State Park's eastern boundary, and state officials have long sought to expand the park's footprint on Perdido Key.

"We're in the very early stages of evaluating whether this parcel aligns with our acquisition priorities," Castillo said. "No formal offer has been made."

The agency's Florida Forever program, which funds conservation land purchases, currently has approximately $100 million available statewide. Castillo would not say whether the Hernandez property had been added to any acquisition list.

A third potential buyer has emerged more quietly. The Perdido Key Association, a nonprofit representing roughly 1,200 property owners on the island, has begun gauging member interest in a community purchase.

"We've had preliminary conversations," said association president David Thornton. "Nothing formal. But there's real appetite among our members to see this stay as some kind of public or semi-public space."

The access question

The sale has surfaced tensions that have simmered on Perdido Key for decades.

The barrier island's development history is one of steady consolidation. In 1970, according to county planning records, Perdido Key had 14 distinct public or quasi-public water access points—fish camps, small marinas, public docks. Today, that number is three: two county-maintained boat ramps and the state park beach.

Every other waterfront parcel has been absorbed into private residential or resort development.

"You used to be able to get to the water a dozen different ways," said Gene Marcum, 79, who has fished Perdido Pass since 1962. Marcum was sitting on an overturned bucket at the Hernandez seawall, a rod propped between his knees. "Now it's all condos and gates. This is it. This is the last one that regular people can use."

The consolidation has been driven by economics that favor density. Waterfront land on Perdido Key now sells for $1.2 to $1.5 million per acre, according to recent comparable sales. A condominium development can generate returns that dwarf anything a fish camp or public amenity could produce.

But some residents argue the math misses something.

"You can't put a dollar value on access," said Rachel Simmons, who lives in the Perdido Dunes subdivision and serves on the county's Coastal Resources Advisory Committee. "Once it's gone, it doesn't come back. You don't get do-overs with waterfront."

The county's role

Escambia County has tools that could influence the property's future, though using them would require political will that hasn't always been present.

The county's land conservation fund, financed by a dedicated portion of tourist development tax revenue, has approximately $3.1 million available for acquisitions, according to budget documents. That's well short of the asking price, but could be combined with state or federal funds.

County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Perdido Key, said he was aware of the sale but had not taken a position.

"I'd want to see what the state's appetite is first," Bergosh said. "If DEP is serious, that's probably the best outcome for everyone. I don't think the county has the resources to do this alone."

Commissioner Lumon May, who chairs the board's infrastructure committee, was more direct.

"We've watched waterfront access disappear on this island for 40 years," May said. "At some point you have to decide if you're going to do something about it or just keep writing reports."

May said he would support using county conservation funds as a match for a state acquisition, but acknowledged the timeline was uncertain. DEP's evaluation process typically takes six to twelve months.

What the developers see

From a development perspective, the Hernandez property offers rare advantages.

Most Perdido Key parcels are narrow slivers running from Gulf beach to bay. The Hernandez tract is wider, with pass frontage that provides both deep-water access and views that condo buyers pay premium prices for.

A development source familiar with the site, who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly, said the property could support a 40- to 50-unit project with underground parking, even after wetland and setback constraints.

"You're talking about $15 to $18 million in sellable units," the source said. "Maybe more depending on how the market moves. That's real money for a $4 million land basis."

The source said they expected multiple developers to submit offers within 60 days.

'He would hate this'

Carmen Hernandez says she tries not to think about what her father would say.

Miguel Hernandez Sr. died in 1991, before the condo towers redrew Perdido Key's silhouette. He never saw the traffic that now chokes the single road onto the island on summer weekends, or the private beach signs that proliferate along shorelines he once considered common ground.

"He would hate this," Carmen Hernandez said. "All of it. The prices, the walls, the way everything belongs to somebody now."

She said the family has not yet decided how to evaluate offers. Price will matter, but so will intent.

"If someone wants to build another tower, I can't stop them," she said. "But I don't have to make it easy."

The pelicans on the seawall shifted and resettled. The bait freezer hummed. Somewhere out in the pass, a mullet jumped.

"Sixty-seven years," Carmen Hernandez said. "That's got to count for something."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's new flight simulator contract could bring 200 jobs—but not until 2028
articles.dek: The Navy's $340 million training modernization deal with a Texas defense contractor includes a Pensacola facility, though local workforce development programs are scrambling to catch up.
brief: L3Harris Technologies awarded $340 million contract to build advanced flight training simulators at NAS Pensacola
New facility expected to create approximately 200 permanent jobs, with hiring beginning in late 2027
Local workforce boards express concern about pipeline for qualified simulation technicians and engineers
articles.body:
The hangar at NAS Pensacola where student naval aviators first learned to fly in 1914 sits empty most days now. A chain-link fence surrounds it. Pigeons nest in the rafters. But two miles east, on a patch of scrubland near the base's eastern perimeter, orange survey stakes mark where the Navy plans to build something new.

L3Harris Technologies, the Melbourne-based defense contractor, won a $340 million contract last month to construct and operate an advanced flight simulation training facility at the Pensacola installation. The project represents the largest single defense contract award tied to Escambia County in more than a decade.

The catch: ground won't break until spring 2027, the facility won't open until mid-2028, and the 200 jobs the company projects will require skills that local workforce programs aren't yet equipped to teach.

"This is transformational for our region's defense economy," said Scott Luth, president and CEO of FloridaWest Economic Development Alliance, at a press conference announcing the contract. "But we have work to do between now and then."

What the contract includes

The Navy's contract with L3Harris covers design, construction and 10 years of operation for what the service calls the Next Generation Pilot Training System. The Pensacola facility will house 12 full-motion flight simulators capable of replicating conditions for the T-6B Texan II and T-45C Goshawk training aircraft.

According to Naval Air Training Command spokesperson Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Torres, the new simulators will allow student pilots to complete up to 40% of their early flight training in virtual environments before climbing into actual cockpits.

"The technology has reached a point where simulator training provides equivalent learning outcomes for certain maneuvers," Torres said. "This reduces costs, reduces risk, and increases throughput."

The contract also includes maintenance and technical support facilities, a 15,000-square-foot classroom building, and infrastructure upgrades to the base's eastern access road.

L3Harris declined to make executives available for interviews but confirmed in a written statement that the company expects to hire approximately 200 full-time employees for the Pensacola operation. Positions will include simulation engineers, software developers, maintenance technicians and administrative staff.

Starting salaries, according to the statement, will range from $52,000 for entry-level technician roles to $145,000 for senior engineering positions.

The workforce gap

The Navy's timeline gives Escambia County roughly 18 months to develop a pipeline of workers qualified for jobs that don't yet exist here in significant numbers.

CareerSource Escarosa, the regional workforce development board, currently lists no training programs specifically for flight simulation technology. The closest offerings are general electronics technician certifications and computer networking courses at Pensacola State College.

"We knew this was coming," said Marcus Webb, CareerSource Escarosa's executive director. "Defense simulation has been a growth area for years. But knowing something and being ready for it are different things."

Webb said his organization has begun conversations with L3Harris about developing a customized training curriculum. The company has similar partnerships with community colleges near its facilities in Arlington, Texas, and Salt Lake City.

But those programs took years to build. Pensacola has months.

Pensacola State College President Ed Meadows said the school is exploring options to fast-track new certificate programs but faces constraints. "You can't just invent an instructor overnight," Meadows said. "These are specialized fields. We need faculty who understand both the technology and how to teach it."

One possibility under discussion: bringing L3Harris employees to campus as adjunct instructors while the college recruits permanent faculty.

Competition from other bases

The Pensacola facility is one of three the Navy plans to build under the Next Generation Pilot Training System program. Similar installations are slated for NAS Kingsville in Texas and NAS Meridian in Mississippi.

Both of those communities have existing simulation industry workforces. Kingsville sits 40 miles from the L3Harris headquarters in Arlington. Meridian hosts Raytheon's simulation operations center, which employs more than 300 people.

Pensacola's defense sector, while substantial, has historically focused on aviation maintenance and training operations rather than simulation technology. The base employs approximately 16,000 military personnel and 7,400 civilians, according to Navy figures, but few of those civilian jobs involve the software engineering and systems integration work that simulation facilities require.

"We're not starting from zero," said Luth, the economic development official. "We have IHMC. We have the cybersecurity programs at UWF. The talent is here, it's just not organized around this specific opportunity yet."

The Institute for Human and Machine Cognition, a nonprofit research organization headquartered in downtown Pensacola, has worked on simulation and artificial intelligence projects for the Defense Department. But the institute focuses on research rather than the applied technician-level work that will comprise most L3Harris positions.

What happens next

L3Harris must submit final facility designs to the Navy by December 2026. Environmental assessments for the construction site are already complete, according to base officials.

The company plans to begin hiring its Pensacola management team in early 2027. Technical positions will be posted starting in late 2027, with the goal of having a full workforce trained and ready when the facility opens the following summer.

Webb, the workforce board director, said his organization will hold its first planning session with L3Harris representatives next month. He expects a formal training partnership announcement by fall.

For now, the orange survey stakes on the base's eastern edge are the only visible sign of what's coming. Most days, the only visitors are rabbits and the occasional jogger on the perimeter road.

In two years, if everything goes according to plan, the site will house technology that didn't exist when those old hangars were built a century ago. Whether Pensacola will have the workers to run it remains an open question.
